418.t: The multi-band battle tour with Basie, Moten and Chick Webb
418.s: He describes a tour of several bands, including Moten, Chick Webb and Zack Whyte, battling at one-nighters.
418.q: I used to sing pretty regular with the band you know. And -- (inaudible) -- it seems like we teamed up here again and there was a five band tour of (inaudible) -- originally it was Count Basie (PHONETIC) you know.

418.t: The multi-band battle tour with Basie, Moten and Chick Webb
418.s: He describes a tour of several bands battling at one-nighters, with Moten breaking it up with Moten Swing.
418.ch: Early bands, Calloway to Basie and Kansas City (third typescript)
418.q: I used to sing pretty regular with the band you know. And -- (inaudible) -- it seems like we teamed up here again and there was a five band tour of (inaudible) -- originally it was Count Basie (PHONETIC) you know.

418.t: The battle-of-the-bands tour with Kirk, Moten and Chick Webb
418.s: He describes a tour of up to seven bands playing one-nighters in battle format, with Moten breaking it up with Moten Swing.
418.q: After that, I came back here again, and there was a five-band tour of Andy Kirk, Bennie Moten (it was Count Basie, you know, but it was Bennie's band then), Chick Webb... That's three of them. Zack Whyte, that's four. And... First it was more than that many bands. I think we

78.t: Rex Stewart and Benny Carter at Wilberforce; battle against McKinney's Cotton Pickers
78.s: Horace brought cornetist Rex Stewart and Benny Carter, found in Pittsburgh, to Wilberforce. The Collegians won a Detroit Graystone battle of bands against McKinney's Cotton Pickers with 'Singing the Blues'.
78.ch: Starting out in New York and Chicago
78.q: He took the trumpet up, and he plays good trumpet, and he's an excellent arranger. He was excellent, and of course I had the late and great Rex Stewart playing cornet with me in Wilberforce. I took Rex to

78.t: Battles of bands and Randy Brooks with Les Brown at Michigan
78.s: Battles were judged by crowd noise; Fletcher and Casa Loma did college battles. At Michigan, Les Brown's trumpeter Randy Brooks so impressed Fletcher's men that they sat to listen.
78.ch: Starting out in New York and Chicago
78.q: Battles of jazz were great in those days. We don't have those now. They were great. Like Fletcher Henderson and Glen Gray and his Casa Loma band (unintelligible) did thirty-one one-nighters of jazz in battles of music in the universities all over the country, like the University of Illinois,…

78.t: Fletcher beats Casa Loma at the Graystone using stock arrangements
78.s: Against Glen Gray's Casa Loma, Fletcher played simple stocks for two sets, letting his men get angry, then unleashed his specials in the third set and won the crowd.
78.ch: Fletcher as a leader and early bandmates
78.q: he didn't worry. I remember one time Fletcher played a battle of music. I'd like to insert this. Against the Casa Loma Band. This happened in Michigan. And this is a funny thing. He was quite a judge of what we call battling with bands, you know. Okay, this happened in the Greystone Ballroom too.…

86.t: Battle of the bands against Lunceford in Hartford
86.s: The tired Basie band arrived from Pittsburgh and outplayed Lunceford, with Pres in top form.
86.q: So one time when they was having a battle of the bands, we were supposed to battle Jimmy Lunceford. Jimmy Lunceford drove from -- he had come out of the Cotton Club in his bus, oh, he had the big Greyhound air-conditioned bus, in Hartford,

86.t: Rivalry of Lester Young and Herschel Evans; the Goodman battle
86.s: Basie kept the two tenors competing, and Edison recalls beating Benny Goodman's band at Madison Square Garden.
86.ch: Leading the Basie band: music, rivals and recordings
86.q: I can understand you asking that question because Basie’s band was built around Herschel and Lester, and he always kept something going between the two. They loved each other. They respected each other. But Prez liked nobody’s playing but his own. And Herschel was a Coleman Hawkins disciple. He…

115.t: The battle of the bands against Nat Towles at Dreamland
115.s: One night at the Dreamland Ballroom in Omaha Hunter's swinging band beat Nat Towles's better-arranged band because of its drummer.
115.ch: Kansas City, Omaha and Lloyd Hunter
115.q: Well, Nat came to town and he'd been in town for about a couple of months. And so I found out that we were supposed to play a battle against him. And at this time I was playing drums.

115.s: Bands laid in wait, making the other play first and then topping it, and dancers could not be fooled.
115.ch: Kansas City, Omaha and Lloyd Hunter
115.q: Then they'd come back and play a set and they'd play the other set.

174.t: Kansas City contest win and Dixieland versus big-band rivals
174.s: At a Kansas City contest, drummer Baby Lovett told them to play old New Orleans jazz; tuba man Baby Woods's solo on Tiger Rag won it. Fancy-arrangement bands like Sunset Royal came to their dances, but crowds wanted the Dixieland.
174.q: We were playing like Kansas City. I thought we had that contest in Kansas City with Fender Harris' orchestra. And this, a baby, a drummer from here. He's a bright fellow. He looked like white.

622.t: The Austin band's drive against Ashcraft's school bands
622.s: Ashcraft recounts a battle of bands where the Austin band outplayed his and argues the growing beat owed little to New Orleans until the Rhythm Kings.
622.q: No, they did not. And I've often wondered where the influence crept in without their knowing it, and I suspect, of course, it was through Paul Merez and Rapolo, and those fellows. And Brunus. One thing that used to surprise me, I originally played with a little band around a country day school.…

881.t: Dave Peyton's band at the Regal, the McKinney battle and the 165th Army band
881.s: He describes the Regal band, a battle with McKinney's Cotton Pickers, and his Army band and theater training.
881.ch: Learning trombone and the Wisconsin Roof years
881.q: Doc Willow? Yeah. Yeah. And Raymond Valentine. And we had Cass Simpson on piano and accordion. And we had Boris Lovingood. He's from, I think Austin, Texas. And we had the, we had the, five brass. And I think we had four reeds. Two pianists and Snagg Jones on the drum. So we had a battle with this,…

85.t: Battle of the bands with McKinney's Cotton Pickers at the Graystone
85.s: Carter's band beat McKinney's Cotton Pickers in Detroit and he still has the trophy cup.
85.q: Well, at least somebody thought we did. They presented us with the cup, which I think says “King of Jazz” or something, you know, because . . . so that was until Paul Whiteman became King of Jazz.

137.t: The Basie versus Lunceford battle of the bands in Hartford
137.s: He switched bands the night of a Hartford battle of the bands and was interviewed on radio, praising both bands.
137.q: That's about right. And when I joined, the night I was supposed to join Lunceford, they booked the battle of music in Connecticut, something like that, -- no, a little further.

87.t: Battles of music with the Ambassadors from Baltimore
87.s: The Miles band played battles with the Baltimore Ambassadors, with a high-note trumpeter Stevenson who later joined Lunceford and the Horton brothers.
87.ch: Virginia school and first Washington bands
87.q: It must have been '31, '32 -- '31, '30 because I went with Earl Hines right after that. Jimmy Mundy was the first guy to go with Earl Hines. But I'll tell you how this kind of came about. We used to play a battle of music all the time with a band from Baltimore, and this band was called the…

758.t: Battle of the bands in Flint with an old rival
758.s: Roy led the band, and the carnival pianist who had mocked him challenged him; the band beat him with classical arrangements and then a screamer.
758.q: : I ended up with the band... Last gig we played was a gig that I got in Flint, Michigan. And you know what's funny? The guy that used to hate me on that carnival, you know, the piano player who said I'd never make it, he came to Flint, and it was... (?) like that is where I got the gig. Even…

232.t: The battle of the bands against Smiling Billy Stewart's Sarasota Serenaders
232.s: The two bands play at opposite ends of the hall; Roy Milton's vocal on I'll Always Be In Love With You wins the crowd, but Stewart's big band from Florida is stronger and Fields resolves to enlarge his band.
232.ch: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
232.q: We were playing, and they managed to see how the people liked you. I would set up one end of the hall and (inaudible) set up the other end of the hall. So you'd play a number and if you got a hand, the people would crowd around you, and this and that and listen to the other band playing like that…

99.t: Battle of music with the Sunset Royal band in Cincinnati
99.s: The Pillars band outplays Florida's Sunset Royal in a battle, its big tones overwhelming their comedy-routine show band.
99.q: You missed it, that's right. That was 1938. We played -- we left here and went to Cincinnati, Ohio. The band was hitting real good. The band was hitting, I mean,

388.t: Ballrooms and Battles of Music with Shaw
388.s: Territory bands played for the Schribmans' ballrooms and colleges; Leeman describes Battles of Music, Shaw against Bunny Berigan and Red Norvo.
388.q: No, I'm just a little bit later on -- because they were all around, the territory bands, they called them territory bands because they played for the Shripmans, and it's their territory, but there were lots of colleges to play in then and ballrooms -- oh, just ballrooms galore, all over -- those…

237.t: Winning the battle of bands over Moten and Andy Kirk
237.s: Goodwin and Lovett recall the band entering in uniform, winning the crowd, and beating Moten's band, Andy Kirk and others.

171.t: Labor Day battle of the bands in Kansas City
171.s: He recalls bands like Bennie Moten, Blue Devils, Trent and George E. Lee, and a later battle against Duke Ellington.
171.ch: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
171.q: Many days after Bennie died, well, Andy Kirk took it and ran away with it But Blue Devils was always bad. Southern Seranades was a powerful group. In those days, see, it was T. Holder instead of Andy Kirk. But Bennie was the boss then.

103.t: Moten's New York visit and the battle of bands tours
103.s: Jones says Walter Page joined Moten in 1932 and describes five-band battle-of-bands tours with Chick Webb and others.
103.q: Walter Page did not join it till 1932. When Bennie came to New York City he upset New York City with "Driving Me Crazy," which was Moten's Swing they played, then. And that's the time when they had the 5-band tour with Blanche Calloway, Johnson (Happy Pals) (Hakapais?), Chick Webb. Everybody would…

473.t: Little Harlem in Buffalo: the on-air battle with Stuff Smith
473.s: A small band grew to seven with John L. Henderson and Joe Thomas; on a radio half hour they battled Stuff Smith's band three blocks away at Little Harlem, and each copied the other's arrangements.
473.ch: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
473.q: And I worked there for awhile. We were five pieces in there. They had four rhythm and myself, and then in come John L. Henderson on alto, and Joe Thomas on the tenor.
